item.title: Postmortem: When df -h Lies — 5.71M Files Burned All Inodes
item.author: blog@baifan.site (ByF (BaiFan))
item.description: A sudden production incident took down the user authentication system: gateways threw 502 Bad Gateway, while the auth service (Casdoor) returned persistent 503 Service Unavailable. Checking the root partition with df -h showed only 40% disk utilization, with 55GB of free space remaining. Yet system calls across the host crashed with no space left on device (ENOSPC). The culprit was a 6-month-old legacy PHP container. Bypassing broken garbage collection and battered by anonymous crawlers, it quietly generated 5.71 million zero-byte session files in a single flat directory, devouring all 6.35 million inodes available on the host filesystem.

item.title: All the Tmux You'll Ever Use: Sessions, Panes, Detach
item.author: blog@baifan.site (ByF (BaiFan))
item.description:
You SSH into a server to run a long task, the network drops, and the task is gone. Tmux exists to solve exactly this — it decouples the terminal session from the window, so the process keeps running after you close the terminal.

The Core Problem It Solves
#

An ordinary terminal window is bound to its processes. Close the window and the processes die. Same story when SSH drops.

item.title: Linux Memory Optimization: ZRAM Principles and Configuration
item.author: blog@baifan.site (ByF (BaiFan))
item.description:
On memory-constrained VPS instances or embedded Linux devices, relying on disk-backed SWAP triggers swap thrashing and system stalls. Using the Linux kernel’s ZRAM to allocate a compressed in-memory block device trades microsecond-level CPU cycles for effectively doubled RAM headroom.

What SWAP Really Is: Faking Memory with Disk
#

SWAP is simple — data that no longer fits in memory gets written to disk and read back when needed. The problem is the word “disk”.

item.title: VPS and Network Infrastructure Jargon Reference
item.author: blog@baifan.site (ByF (BaiFan))
item.description:
The VPS and datacenter hosting ecosystem features specialized terminology spanning virtualization architectures, transit routing protocols, and peer community jargon.

People and Identity
#

MJJ
#

Originally referred to users hanging around the Hostloc forum; now a blanket term for anyone obsessed with tinkering with VPSes. It comes from a Hostloc forum meme, short for 买鸡鸡/没鸡鸡 (“bought a chicken / no chicken” — interpret it however you like). It started as a slur but gradually evolved into a self-deprecating badge of in-group identity, and in most contexts today it carries no malice (though some also use MJJ for players who pay little and demand much).
